pg-indexes.md:
## Why it exists
A table with 10 million rows has no built-in order. To find one user by email, Postgres must read every row: a **sequential scan**. An **index** is a separate sorted structure that lets it jump straight to the matching rows, turning seconds into milliseconds.

## Mental model
The index at the back of a book: instead of reading every page to find a topic, you look it up alphabetically and get the page numbers.

{{dg:0}}

## How it works
The default index type is a **B-tree**: a balanced tree of sorted pages. A lookup walks from root to leaf in a handful of steps, so cost grows with the logarithm of the table size, not the size itself. The **query planner** estimates costs from table statistics and picks the cheaper plan, which is not always the index: if a filter matches most of the table (low **selectivity**), reading the whole table sequentially is faster.

## Worked example
```sql
CREATE TABLE users (id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, email text NOT NULL, created_at timestamptz DEFAULT now());
-- after loading a few million rows:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'ana@example.com';
-- Seq Scan on users ... Execution Time: ~900 ms

CREATE INDEX users_email_idx ON users (email);
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'ana@example.com';
-- Index Scan using users_email_idx ... Execution Time: ~0.1 ms
```
Timings are illustrative; yours depend on data size and hardware.

## In real products
- A **composite index** for a feed: `CREATE INDEX ON posts (user_id, created_at DESC)` serves `WHERE user_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20` without a separate sort. Column order matters: equality columns first, then the sort column.
- A **partial index** for soft deletes: `CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` stays small and fast.
- A **GIN index** for `jsonb` containment and full-text search.

## Trade-offs
| Index type | Best for | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| B-tree | Equality, ranges, sorting | Slower writes, extra disk |
| Hash | Equality only | Rarely better than B-tree |
| GIN | jsonb, arrays, full-text | Slow to update |
| BRIN | Huge, naturally ordered tables | Coarse; only helps if data is ordered |

> [!pitfall] Wrapping an indexed column in a function, like `WHERE lower(email) = 'x'`, bypasses the index. Create an expression index on `lower(email)` instead.

> [!tip] Every index slows inserts and updates. Drop unused ones: check `pg_stat_user_indexes` for indexes with zero scans.

## Debugging
Always read the plan: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` shows the scan type, actual rows and time. A Seq Scan on a big table with a selective filter is the signal to look for a missing index.
q: Why might Postgres ignore an index for a query?
If the filter matches a large share of rows a sequential scan is cheaper; also when the column is wrapped in a function or statistics are stale.
For `WHERE user_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC`, what column order should a composite index use?
`(user_id, created_at DESC)`: the equality column first, then the sort column.

pg-transactions.md:
## Why it exists
A bank transfer is two updates: subtract from one account, add to another. If the server crashes between them, money vanishes. A **transaction** groups statements so they all happen or none do, and other sessions never see the half-finished state.

## ACID in one breath
- **Atomicity:** all or nothing.
- **Consistency:** constraints hold before and after.
- **Isolation:** concurrent transactions do not trample each other.
- **Durability:** once committed, it survives a crash (the write-ahead log makes this possible).

{{dg:0}}

## How Postgres does it: MVCC
Postgres never overwrites a row in place. An UPDATE writes a new **row version**, and readers see the version that was current when their snapshot began. So readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers. Old versions are cleaned up later by **vacuum**.

## Worked example
```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;   -- or ROLLBACK; to undo both
```
Use the atomic form `balance = balance - 100`, not read-then-write in application code. Two requests reading the same balance would both write stale results (a lost update).

## Isolation levels
| Level | What you may see | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Read Committed (default) | Each statement sees data committed before it started | Good default; non-repeatable reads possible |
| Repeatable Read | One snapshot for the whole transaction | May fail with a serialization error; retry |
| Serializable | As if transactions ran one at a time | Highest safety; be ready to retry |

## Locks and queues
`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` locks the rows you read so no one else changes them until you finish. With `SKIP LOCKED` it makes a safe job queue:
```sql
SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'pending'
ORDER BY id LIMIT 1
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
```
Each worker grabs a different row without waiting for the others.

> [!pitfall] Two transactions that lock rows in opposite order cause a deadlock, and Postgres aborts one. Lock in a consistent order and retry on error 40P01.
> [!pitfall] Long-open transactions (a forgotten BEGIN in a shell, an idle pooled connection) keep old row versions alive, bloat tables and block vacuum.
> [!tip] Retry on serialization failures (40001) and deadlocks (40P01), and make the retried operation idempotent so running it twice is harmless.
q: Why is `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100` safer than reading the balance and writing it back?
The database applies the change atomically to the current row, avoiding a lost update when two requests run at once.
What problem does SKIP LOCKED solve?
It lets many workers pull different jobs from the same table without blocking on rows another worker already locked.

schema-design.md:
## Why it exists
Schemas outlive code. A wrong table shape leaks into every query, API and migration for years. Good design stores each fact once, lets the database enforce rules, and leaves room to change.

{{dg:0}}

## Normalization in practice
- **1NF:** one value per column, no comma-separated lists. Use a child table, or an array or `jsonb` only when you really treat it as a blob.
- **2NF and 3NF:** every column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key. If `orders` stores `customer_email`, move it to `customers`.
- **Denormalize on purpose** for read speed (a counter column, a cached total), and know what keeps the copy correct.

## Worked example
```sql
CREATE TABLE customers (
  id         uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  email      text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  status      text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('pending','paid','shipped','cancelled')),
  total_cents integer NOT NULL CHECK (total_cents >= 0),
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC);
```
Note the choices: `timestamptz` for time, integer cents for money, a `CHECK` instead of trusting the app, and an index on the foreign key (Postgres does not create one automatically).

## Keys and constraints
| Choice | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| bigint identity | Small, fast, ordered | Guessable, awkward across systems |
| uuid (v4) | Unguessable, generated anywhere | Larger, random insert order |
| Natural key (email) | Meaningful | Real-world values change |

Use constraints for rules the database can enforce: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, FOREIGN KEY. They are the last line of defense when a bug slips past your app.

## In real products
- **Multi-tenancy:** add `tenant_id` to every table, index it, and enforce isolation with Row Level Security.
- **Soft delete:** a `deleted_at` column plus partial indexes `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`; unique constraints must account for it.
- **Audit trail:** `created_at`, `updated_at` and `created_by` on important tables.
- **Evolving safely:** expand and contract migrations. Add a nullable column, backfill, enforce, then drop the old one.

> [!pitfall] Storing money in `float` produces rounding errors. Use integer minor units (cents) or `numeric`.
> [!pitfall] `timestamp` without time zone silently drops zone information. Use `timestamptz` and store UTC.
> [!tip] Name things consistently: plural tables, singular columns, an `_id` suffix for foreign keys, all lowercase snake_case so you never need quoting.
q: Why add an index on a foreign key column?
Postgres does not create one automatically; without it, joins and ON DELETE checks scan the child table.
Give one reason to denormalize and one risk.
Reads get faster (no join or aggregation); the risk is the copies drifting out of sync unless something keeps them updated.

sql-basics.md:
## Why it exists

Almost every product you will touch keeps its important data in a **relational database**: users, orders, payments, permissions, messages. **SQL** (Structured Query Language) is the language for asking such a database questions and changing its contents, and it has been the standard for about fifty years. Learning it from zero pays off immediately: analysts, back-end engineers, data engineers, product managers and support teams all use it, and an ORM or a BI tool is only a thin layer that generates SQL anyway.

SQL is **declarative**: you describe the result you want ("paid orders per customer, biggest first") and the database's **query planner** decides how to get it (which indexes to use, in what order to join). You do not write loops. That is why one short query can replace a page of code, and why you must understand *what the question means* rather than *how to compute it*.

**Mental model:** a table is a spreadsheet with strict rules. Rows are records, columns have names and types, and a **primary key** uniquely identifies each row. Tables point at each other through **foreign keys** (an order stores the id of its customer instead of copying the customer's name). Queries combine and filter these tables into a new temporary table, the **result set**.

{{dg:0}}

## How it works

All examples below were run against one small shop database, so you can follow along in any SQLite shell (`sqlite3` is a single file, nothing to install on most systems; Python ships a `sqlite3` module). PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server use the same core language with small differences, listed at the end.

### Tables, keys and types (DDL)

**DDL** (data definition language: `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`) defines the structure. **DML** (data manipulation: `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`) changes rows. Queries (`SELECT`) read them.

```sql
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;   -- SQLite only: foreign keys are OFF by default there

CREATE TABLE customers (
  id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name    TEXT NOT NULL,
  email   TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  country TEXT NOT NULL,
  vip     INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (vip IN (0, 1))
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),
  placed_on   TEXT NOT NULL,   -- ISO date 'YYYY-MM-DD'
  status      TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'paid', 'refunded')),
  total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (total_cents >= 0),
  coupon      TEXT             -- NULL means "no coupon"
);

INSERT INTO customers (name, email, country, vip) VALUES
  ('Ada',    'ada@example.com',    'UK', 1),
  ('Bashir', 'bashir@example.com', 'NG', 0),
  ('Chen',   'chen@example.com',   'CN', 0),
  ('Dalia',  'dalia@example.com',  'SA', 1),
  ('Emil',   'emil@example.com',   'DE', 0);

INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, placed_on, status, total_cents, coupon) VALUES
  (1, '2026-01-05', 'paid',     12000, 'SAVE10'),
  (1, '2026-02-11', 'paid',      8000, NULL),
  (2, '2026-02-14', 'pending',   4500, NULL),
  (3, '2026-02-20', 'refunded',  3000, 'HALF'),
  (4, '2026-03-02', 'paid',     25000, NULL),
  (4, '2026-03-15', 'paid',      5000, 'SAVE10'),
  (1, '2026-03-20', 'paid',     15000, NULL),
  (2, '2026-03-25', 'paid',      7000, 'WELCOME');
```

Notes on the design: money is stored as **integer cents** (never floating point, because `0.1 + 0.2` is not `0.3` in binary); `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`, `CHECK` and `REFERENCES` are **constraints**, rules the database enforces for every writer, including bugs, scripts and future teammates. Constraints are the cheapest data-quality tool you have.

### SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT

```sql
SELECT name, country FROM customers WHERE country IN ('UK', 'SA') ORDER BY name;
-- result: name | country
--   Ada | UK
--   Dalia | SA

SELECT id, total_cents / 100.0 AS total
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid' AND total_cents >= 10000
ORDER BY total_cents DESC
LIMIT 2;
-- result: id | total
--   5 | 250.0
--   7 | 150.0

SELECT name FROM customers WHERE email LIKE '%@example.com' AND name LIKE '_a%';
-- result: name
--   Bashir
--   Dalia
```

`SELECT` picks columns (and computes new ones with `AS` aliases), `FROM` names the table, `WHERE` keeps matching rows. Combine tests with `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`, and add parentheses when mixing them (`AND` binds tighter than `OR`). `IN (...)`, `BETWEEN a AND b` and `LIKE` (`%` is any text, `_` one character) cover most filters. `ORDER BY` sorts; **without it the row order is not guaranteed**, and the same goes for `LIMIT`, so always pair them.

### NULL: "unknown", not zero

`NULL` means the value is missing or unknown. Any comparison with `NULL` yields *unknown*, which `WHERE` treats as false. So `= NULL` never matches; use `IS NULL`.

```sql
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE coupon = NULL;      -- always empty!
-- result: id
--   (no rows)
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE coupon IS NULL ORDER BY id;
-- result: id
--   2
--   3
--   5
--   7
SELECT id, COALESCE(coupon, 'none') AS coupon_label FROM orders WHERE id <= 3;
-- result: id | coupon_label
--   1 | SAVE10
--   2 | none
--   3 | none
SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_rows, COUNT(coupon) AS with_coupon FROM orders;
-- result: all_rows | with_coupon
--   8 | 4
SELECT 1 = NULL AS a, NULL = NULL AS b, NULL IS NULL AS c, 1 NOT IN (2, NULL) AS d;
-- result: a | b | c | d
--   NULL | NULL | 1 | NULL
```

`COALESCE(a, b)` returns the first non-NULL value. `COUNT(*)` counts rows; `COUNT(column)` counts non-NULL values. The last query shows the classic trap: `x NOT IN (list containing NULL)` is never true, so a subquery such as `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT parent_id FROM t)` silently returns nothing when any `parent_id` is NULL. Use `NOT EXISTS` instead.

### Aggregates, GROUP BY and HAVING

**Aggregate functions** (`COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`) collapse many rows into one value. `GROUP BY` makes one result row per group, and `HAVING` filters the *groups* after aggregating, while `WHERE` filters *rows* before.

```sql
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(total_cents) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(total_cents) > 10000
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
-- result: customer_id | orders | revenue
--   1 | 3 | 35000
--   4 | 2 | 30000
```

Remember the **logical order** the database follows, which explains most "why can't I use that here" errors: `FROM/JOIN` → `WHERE` → `GROUP BY` → `HAVING` → `SELECT` → `ORDER BY` → `LIMIT`. `WHERE` runs before `SELECT`, so it cannot use your column aliases; `ORDER BY` runs after, so it can.

### Joins: combining tables

A **join** matches rows from two tables on a condition. `INNER JOIN` keeps only matching pairs; `LEFT JOIN` keeps every row from the left table and fills the right side with NULLs when nothing matches. That makes `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL` the standard way to find "rows with no match". (The SQL joins lesson goes deeper on join types and performance.)

```sql
SELECT c.name, SUM(o.total_cents) / 100.0 AS paid_total
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY c.id
ORDER BY paid_total DESC;
-- result: name | paid_total
--   Ada | 350.0
--   Dalia | 300.0
--   Bashir | 70.0

SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id
ORDER BY orders DESC, c.name;
-- result: name | orders
--   Ada | 3
--   Bashir | 2
--   Dalia | 2
--   Chen | 1
--   Emil | 0

SELECT c.name FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL;
-- result: name
--   Emil
```

Count `o.id`, not `*`, in the left-join query: `COUNT(*)` would count the NULL-filled row for a customer with no orders as 1.

### Changing data: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, upsert, transactions

```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid' WHERE id = 3 RETURNING id, status;
-- result: id | status
--   3 | paid
COMMIT;

INSERT INTO customers (name, email, country)
VALUES ('Bashir Ali', 'bashir@example.com', 'EG')
ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET name = excluded.name, country = excluded.country;
SELECT id, name, country FROM customers WHERE email = 'bashir@example.com';
-- result: id | name | country
--   2 | Bashir Ali | EG

DELETE FROM orders WHERE id = 4 RETURNING id, status;
-- result: id | status
--   4 | refunded
```

- **`UPDATE` and `DELETE` without `WHERE` change every row.** Before running one, run the same `WHERE` as a `SELECT` and look at the count; run changes inside a **transaction** (`BEGIN ... COMMIT`, or `ROLLBACK` to undo) so a mistake can be cancelled.
- A **transaction** groups statements so they all happen or none do (the "A" in ACID); two orders being paid at once cannot corrupt each other.
- **Upsert** (`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` in SQLite and PostgreSQL; `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` in MySQL) inserts or updates in one atomic statement, which avoids the race in "check, then insert".
- `RETURNING` hands back the affected rows (SQLite 3.35+, PostgreSQL), saving a second query.

Constraints reject bad writes, and the error tells you which rule fired:

```sql
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, placed_on, status, total_cents) VALUES (99, '2026-04-01', 'paid', 100);
-- error: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed
UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped' WHERE id = 1;
-- error: CHECK constraint failed: status IN ('pending', 'paid', 'refunded')
INSERT INTO customers (name, email, country) VALUES ('Dup', 'ada@example.com', 'UK');
-- error: UNIQUE constraint failed: customers.email
```

### Views and indexes

A **view** is a saved query you can select from like a table; it stores no data (a *materialized view* does, in PostgreSQL). An **index** is a sorted lookup structure on one or more columns that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table. Primary keys and `UNIQUE` constraints create one automatically. Add indexes for columns used in `WHERE`, `JOIN` and `ORDER BY` on big tables; each one speeds reads and slows writes and uses disk. PostgreSQL does **not** index foreign key columns for you.

```sql
CREATE VIEW paid_orders AS
SELECT id, customer_id, placed_on, total_cents FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid';

SELECT COUNT(*) AS paid_count, SUM(total_cents) AS paid_cents FROM paid_orders;
-- result: paid_count | paid_cents
--   7 | 76500

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders (customer_id);
```

{{dg:1}}

## Worked example

The business asks three questions. Each is a single query over the same data.

**1. Revenue per month (paid orders only).** `substr` is SQLite's way to take the first seven characters (`2026-03`); in PostgreSQL you would write `date_trunc('month', placed_on)`.

```sql
SELECT substr(placed_on, 1, 7) AS month, SUM(total_cents) / 100.0 AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month;
-- result: month | revenue
--   2026-01 | 120.0
--   2026-02 | 125.0
--   2026-03 | 520.0
```

**2. VIP customers and how much each has spent**, including those with no paid orders yet (a `LEFT JOIN` with the status test in the join condition, so non-paid orders do not remove the customer):

```sql
SELECT c.name, c.vip, COALESCE(SUM(o.total_cents), 0) / 100.0 AS paid_total
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid'
WHERE c.vip = 1
GROUP BY c.id
ORDER BY paid_total DESC;
-- result: name | vip | paid_total
--   Ada | 1 | 350.0
--   Dalia | 1 | 300.0
```

**3. Calling SQL safely from code.** Never build SQL by gluing user text into a string: that is **SQL injection**. Send the query and the values separately with placeholders (`?` in SQLite, `%s` or `$1` in other drivers), and the database treats the value as data, never as code.

```python
import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.execute("CREATE TABLE users (name TEXT, secret TEXT)")
con.executemany("INSERT INTO users VALUES (?, ?)", [("ada", "a-secret"), ("bob", "b-secret")])

evil = "x' OR '1'='1"
unsafe = con.execute(f"SELECT name, secret FROM users WHERE name = '{evil}'").fetchall()
safe = con.execute("SELECT name, secret FROM users WHERE name = ?", (evil,)).fetchall()
print(len(unsafe), len(safe))   # 2 0: the glued string leaked every row, the placeholder matched nothing
```

## In real products

- **Application back ends** (Django, Rails, Spring, Node with Prisma or Drizzle, SQLAlchemy) generate SQL like the above. When a page is slow, you read the generated SQL, run `EXPLAIN` (PostgreSQL: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`) and add an index or rewrite the query.
- **Analytics and BI** (Metabase, Looker, dbt, BigQuery, Snowflake) are SQL end to end: monthly revenue, funnels and retention are `GROUP BY` queries over fact tables.
- **Migrations** (Flyway, Alembic, Prisma Migrate) are versioned DDL scripts reviewed like code, applied in CI and production in the same order.
- **Reporting replicas:** heavy analytical queries run against a read replica so they cannot slow checkout.
- **Embedded SQLite** powers phone apps, browsers, desktop apps and small production sites; PostgreSQL is the default server database for most new products.

> [!pitfall] `x = NULL` and `x NOT IN (subquery with NULLs)` silently return no rows. Use `IS NULL`, `COALESCE` and `NOT EXISTS`.

> [!pitfall] `UPDATE` or `DELETE` with a forgotten `WHERE`. Run the matching `SELECT` first, wrap the change in `BEGIN ... COMMIT`, and keep backups and point-in-time recovery on in production.

> [!pitfall] Selecting a column that is neither in `GROUP BY` nor aggregated. PostgreSQL rejects it; SQLite quietly returns an arbitrary row's value, which looks right in testing and is wrong in production.

> [!pitfall] `LIMIT` without `ORDER BY` returns arbitrary rows, and big `OFFSET` pagination gets slower the deeper you go. For long lists use keyset pagination: `WHERE id > :last_seen ORDER BY id LIMIT 20`.

> [!tip] Write queries in the logical order (FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, SELECT) and test each step by running the partial query. Name columns explicitly instead of `SELECT *` in application code so adding a column cannot break a consumer or leak a field.

> [!tip] Use the database to guarantee rules: `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`, `CHECK`, foreign keys. Application checks have gaps (a second service, a script, a race); constraints do not.

> [!cost] Indexes cost write speed and storage, `SELECT *` over wide tables costs network and memory, and in cloud warehouses (BigQuery, Snowflake) you often pay per byte scanned, so select only the columns and date ranges you need.

> [!security] Always use parameterised queries, never string-built SQL. Give the application a database user with only the privileges it needs (no `DROP`, no superuser), keep credentials in a secrets manager, and never expose a raw SQL console to untrusted users. Personal data in tables falls under privacy law, so limit who can query it.

> [!prod] Production SQL habits: migrations in version control, a reviewed `EXPLAIN` for new hot queries, statement timeouts, connection pooling, backups with tested restores, and slow-query logs (`pg_stat_statements` in PostgreSQL) reviewed regularly.

> [!version] Verified 2026-10-21: every SQL block above was executed in order against one in-memory SQLite 3.45.1 database in the sandbox (via Python's `sqlite3` module) and the `-- result` and `-- error` comments were generated from the real output; the Python injection example was run too. NOT verified: behaviour on PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQL Server (the dialect differences in this lesson are stated from general knowledge: `date_trunc`, `GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY`, `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`, PostgreSQL's strict `GROUP BY`, no automatic index on foreign keys), `EXPLAIN` output, and performance claims. SQLite is dynamically typed, so type errors that PostgreSQL would raise can pass silently there.
q: Why does WHERE coupon = NULL return no rows?
Comparing anything with NULL gives unknown, which WHERE treats as false. Use IS NULL, or COALESCE, to handle missing values.
What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation, so it can use aggregates such as SUM(total).
How do you stop user input from changing the meaning of a query?
Send the query and the values separately using parameter placeholders, so the database treats input as data and never as SQL text (this prevents SQL injection).

sql-joins.md:
## Why it exists
Relational data is split across tables so nothing is repeated: customers in one table, orders in another. A **join** stitches them back together at query time, so you store each fact once and still ask questions that span tables.

## Mental model
Two lists on a desk. A join lays them side by side, pairing each row of the first with every row of the second where the `ON` condition is true. The join type decides what happens to rows with no partner.

{{dg:0}}

## Worked example
```sql
-- customers(id, name), orders(id, customer_id, total, created_at)
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders, COALESCE(SUM(o.total), 0) AS revenue
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 10;
```
`LEFT JOIN` keeps customers with no orders (their `o.*` columns are NULL), so they show 0 instead of vanishing.

## Join types
| Join | Keeps | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| INNER | Only rows with a match on both sides | You need pairs that exist |
| LEFT | All left rows, matches or NULL | Optional relationships, including rows with no match |
| RIGHT | All right rows | Rare; swap the tables and use LEFT |
| FULL | All rows from both sides | Reconciling two lists |
| CROSS | Every combination | Generating combinations or calendars |

## CTEs and window functions
A **CTE** names a subquery so a long query reads top to bottom. A **window function** computes across related rows without collapsing them like GROUP BY does.
```sql
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT customer_id, date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month, SUM(total) AS spend
  FROM orders GROUP BY 1, 2
)
SELECT customer_id, month, spend,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY month ORDER BY spend DESC) AS rank_in_month
FROM monthly;
```

## In real products
- Dashboards aggregate per user or day with `GROUP BY`, then join to dimension tables for names.
- Feeds join `posts` to `follows` to find what a user should see; index the join columns.
- Deduplication: keep the newest row per email with `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY created_at DESC) = 1`.

> [!pitfall] A condition on the right table in `WHERE` turns a LEFT JOIN into an inner join, because NULL rows fail the test. Put it in the `ON` clause: `LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.total > 100`.
> [!pitfall] Joining a one-to-many table before aggregating multiplies rows and inflates sums. Aggregate in a subquery or CTE first, then join.
> [!tip] `COUNT(*)` counts rows; `COUNT(col)` skips NULLs. After a LEFT JOIN, count a column from the right table to get 0 for no matches.
q: Why does adding `WHERE o.total > 100` after a LEFT JOIN drop customers with no orders?
Unmatched rows have NULL in o.total, and NULL > 100 is not true, so they are filtered out. Move the condition into the ON clause.
When would you use a window function instead of GROUP BY?
When you need a per-row result that depends on related rows, such as a rank or running total, without collapsing the rows.
